entities.name: Priscus of Epirus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Priscus of Epirus, also known as Priscus the Thesprotian and Priscus the Molossian, was a prominent Neoplatonist philosopher and theurgist who flourished in the mid-4th century CE. Born in Epirus, a region in northwestern Greece, Priscus became a leading figure within the Iamblichean school of Neoplatonism, which emphasized theurgical rituals alongside philosophical contemplation as a path to divine union. His significance lies in his close association with Emperor Julian (r. 361–363 CE), whom he served as a philosophical mentor and confidant, playing a crucial role in the emperor's ambitious, albeit short-lived, pagan revival efforts across the Roman Empire.

Priscus's intellectual career saw him teaching in Ephesus, a vibrant intellectual hub of the late Roman world, where he collaborated with other notable Neoplatonists like Maximus of Ephesus. Their collective influence on Julian was profound, particularly in shaping the emperor's commitment to restoring traditional Greco-Roman polytheism and promoting Neoplatonic philosophy as its intellectual bedrock. Priscus accompanied Julian on his campaigns, including the ill-fated Persian expedition of 363 CE, offering counsel and participating in the emperor's attempts to re-establish pagan cults and institutions. Following Julian's death, Priscus, unlike some of his colleagues, managed to survive the subsequent Christian backlash, testament to either his discretion or perhaps his less overtly political involvement compared to figures like Maximus.
